title: “Biases of Aspiring Psychotherapists”: Preferences and Motivations for Therapy Toward Patients with Different Characteristics
summary:
Many people with mental health issues have difficulty finding a spot in therapy. Those with more complex issues or certain personal characteristics are particularly affected. This may be due to therapists’ uncertainties, limited treatment options, or even unconscious biases.

This study examines whether prospective psychotherapists vary in their willingness to treat certain patients. Of particular interest is whether this willingness depends on the type of problems a person has, how motivated they are to change, whether they are religious, or what their sexual orientation is. Such differences could result in some people having poorer access to psychotherapy. The study also examines how confident the participants feel about being able to help these individuals.

The study is conducted using an online questionnaire. After a brief check of the eligibility criteria, participants are shown, one after another, brief descriptions of fictional patients who differ in specific characteristics. For each description, participants indicate how willing they would be to treat that person and how confident they are in their ability to help. In addition, some general information about the person as well as assessments of their own preparedness in dealing with different patient groups are collected.

Participation in this study is intended to encourage participants to reflect on their own attitudes and any uncertainties they may have when interacting with patients. At the same time, it aims to help to understand potential barriers to accessing psychotherapy and to lay the groundwork for improvements in training and care.
conditions: The study investigates potential inequalities in access to outpatient psychotherapy as a health-related issue. Specifically, it examines whether certain patient groups such as individuals with complex mental health conditions (e.g., borderline personality disorder, substance use disorder, post-traumatic stress disorder), varying levels of treatment motivation, different degrees of religiosity, or different sexual orientations—may experience reduced treatment willingness and lower perceived treatability by (future) psychotherapists. These differences may contribute to disparities in mental health care provision and access.
